name: publish-subscribe-channel
intent: Deliver each published event to every interested receiver by fanning it out into one copy per subscriber, so the publisher broadcasts without knowing who - or how many - consumers exist.
problem: One event must reach an unknown and changing set of independent consumers. A point-to-point channel hands each message to exactly one receiver, and direct calls couple the publisher to every consumer it must notify, so each new reaction forces an edit to the publisher.
context: Event-driven integration and notification, in-process or brokered: several independent components react to the same business or system event, subscriptions are added and removed at runtime, and the publisher must stay ignorant of the consumer set. Applies to in-process event buses as well as broker topics; the delivery guarantees (durability, ordering, overflow) are chosen per subscription and are not supplied by the pattern itself.
benefits: Fan-out semantics: every current subscriber receives its own copy, so one publish serves an arbitrary number of reactions.
Publisher decoupling: the publisher addresses only the channel - subscriber identities, count and availability are unknown to it.
Runtime extensibility: new consumers (audit, search indexing, analytics, monitoring) subscribe without touching the publisher or the existing subscribers.
Independent copies: in brokered realizations each subscription owns its queue and acknowledgements, so one consumer's failure does not consume or corrupt another's copy.
Eavesdropping for observability: an extra subscriber can mirror channel traffic for logging or diagnostics without disturbing the existing flow.
Per-subscription durability: transient subscribers receive only live messages, while durable subscribers retain what was published while they were offline.
tradeoffs: Every publish costs one copy per subscriber plus one retained buffer slot per subscriber: fan-out work and memory grow with the number of subscriptions.

Slow-subscriber problem: a lagging consumer forces a policy - retain (memory), drop oldest/newest, or disconnect the laggard - so the channel leaks or loses messages unless the overflow policy is chosen and documented.

Non-durable subscribers silently miss every message published while they are offline; closing that gap needs durable subscriptions or guaranteed delivery, which reintroduces broker storage and retention cost.
The consumer set is dynamic and may be unknown at design time: the effects of publishing cannot be read off the code, which makes impact analysis, debugging and governance harder (event soup).
There is no global ordering and delivery is usually at-least-once, so subscribers must tolerate duplicates and arrival interleaved with unrelated events.

Synchronous in-process dispatchers (C# events, EventEmitter, EventTarget) make publisher latency and failure modes depend on subscriber code: one subscriber that blocks or throws affects the rest of the notification.
Subscriptions are a data-exposure surface - every event on a topic reaches every subscriber - so widening the audience requires message filtering or a separate channel.

participants.responsibility: Announces an event by publishing a message to the channel; it holds no reference to any subscriber and never decides who receives it.

One input that splits into one logical output per subscription: delivers a copy of each published message to each subscriber and owns the delivery contract (retention, ordering, overflow, acknowledgement).
The registration binding a subscriber to the channel; owns that subscriber's copy queue and delivery state, and makes the difference between transient (live-only) and durable (retained) interest.
Registers interest and consumes its own copy of each message once, independently of the other subscribers; it never talks back to the publisher on the same channel.
The event or document payload that is copied per subscriber; it must be treated as immutable, because all copies start from the same published value.

Mediates the channel between processes in brokered realizations: persists messages, manages subscriptions and acknowledgements. Absent in in-process event buses, where the channel is a language construct.

use_cases: In-process domain events: the order service announces 'order placed'; billing, inventory, notification and audit each react on their own subscription.

Cross-service integration over a broker topic: one event is published once and every subscribing service, with its own subscription, receives an independent copy (Kafka topic, Google Cloud Pub/Sub topic, JMS topic).
UI and plugin platforms: DOM events, framework lifecycle events and named application events consumed by any number of widgets, plugins or extensions.
Cache invalidation and configuration refresh: one change is broadcast so every node drops its stale entry instead of polling.
Observability taps: a logging, auditing or message-store subscriber mirrors all traffic on a channel without altering publishers or consumers.
Market data, telemetry and sensor feeds: identical updates must reach many independent analytical consumers.

Apache Kafka: publishing to a topic and assigning each independent downstream application its own consumer group gives pub-sub fan-out, while consumers within one group share partitions as competing consumers.
Amazon SNS to SQS fan-out: one SNS topic publishes a notification to multiple SQS queue subscriptions, giving each downstream worker an independently retained copy.
Azure Service Bus topics and subscriptions: each subscription acts as a virtual queue receiving its own topic copy, with per-subscription filters for selective fan-out.
avoid_when: Exactly one consumer may process each message (work distribution, throughput scaling): use a Point-to-Point Channel with Competing Consumers instead.
A single caller is waiting for an answer: use Request-Reply or a direct method call, not a broadcast.
The receivers are few, fixed and known at design time and the publisher may hold references: plain callbacks or Observer are simpler than a channel with a registry.
Strict global ordering, exactly-once processing or transactional coupling between the publisher and all subscribers is required: use a log or transactional store, not a pub-sub channel.
Fan-out would multiply work with no independent consumer (broadcasting internal value changes to unrelated components): wire the dependency explicitly instead.
anti_patterns: "Topic as RPC": publishing a message and expecting a reply or confirmation that every subscriber processed it - a publish-subscribe channel has no return path.
Sharing one mutable payload object with all in-process subscribers, so one subscriber's mutation changes what the others observe.
Registering subscribers with no unsubscribe path or scope, producing listener leaks and duplicate handling after components are recreated.
A global stringly-typed event bus with no schema, naming convention or topic owner - the event soup nobody can version, secure or debug.
Assuming each subscriber sees each message exactly once while the transport is at-least-once: non-idempotent subscribers then double-charge, double-send or double-apply.
design_principles: Dependency inversion: the publisher depends on the channel abstraction and never on subscriber types.
Open/closed principle: new reactions arrive by subscription, not by editing the publisher.
Single responsibility: the channel owns copy, fan-out and delivery policy; subscribers own reaction logic only.
Loose coupling: referential, temporal and platform decoupling between publisher and subscribers.
Explicit contract: durability, ordering, overflow and acknowledgement semantics are part of the channel's interface, not implementation trivia.
best_practices: Treat published messages as immutable and give each subscriber its own copy or a frozen value.
Declare the delivery contract per subscription: transient vs durable, bounded buffer size, overflow policy, acknowledgement and retry expectations.
Keep subscriber queues independent; one blocked consumer must not stall the publisher or its peers.
Unsubscribe deterministically (scoped registration, disposal tokens, weak references) so long-lived channels do not keep dead subscribers alive.
Name and version topics and event schemas explicitly, keep an owner per topic, and validate payloads at the boundary.
Write subscribers idempotent and order-tolerant: assume at-least-once delivery and per-subscriber ordering only.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003) - Publish-Subscribe Channel (Messaging Channels chapter).
